name: Twinkie diet

lead: The Twinkie diet is the nickname for a 2010 experiment by Kansas State University nutrition professor Mark Haub, who ate snack foods such as Twinkies, Oreos and Doritos at regular intervals while keeping his total calories low. He lost 27 pounds (about 12 kg) over two months and his body mass index returned to the normal range [1].

In lifting and physique communities the story is used as a reference point for the idea that fat loss follows calorie intake, which is what gets people leaner and shows more muscle definition. Posters on T Nation bring it up when arguing that any structured reduction in intake produces weight loss [2][3].

paras: In the original experiment, a snack-cake or similar item was eaten every few hours in place of regular meals, alongside a daily protein shake, a vegetable serving, and a multivitamin; he also ate vegetables with his family at dinner [1]. Community members mostly mention it as an example in diet debates rather than as something they follow.

Haub's experiment was a single person monitored by himself, and it did not test long-term health outcomes. Forum commenters point out that the baseline population is often unhealthy and that a controlled-portion diet of any kind would likely help it [3]. Nutrition and micronutrient quality are separate from calorie quantity, which the experiment did not isolate.

angle.text: The Twinkie diet is used as an illustration that calorie deficit is the main driver of weight loss, so people who want a leaner look cite it when justifying flexible, quantity-focused dieting. It is a demonstration of the principle rather than a plan with a following of its own.

lead: The Twinkie diet is the popular name for a 2010 self-experiment by Mark Haub, a professor of human nutrition at Kansas State University. He ate a snack of Twinkies, Oreos or Doritos about every three hours, with the aim of showing students that calorie counting matters most for weight loss, regardless of the nutritional quality of the food [1].

Despite the name, his intake was not only junk food: he also had a daily protein shake, a serving of canned green beans or celery, a multivitamin, milk, carrots and fortified cereal [1]. He lost 27 pounds over two months and his body mass index moved back into the normal range [1].

For people trying to look leaner, the experiment is cited as a demonstration of energy balance: sustained intake below expenditure reduces body fat, which reveals muscle and sharpens facial and body definition. In physique forums it is used in discussions of flexible dieting, and in arguments over whether food quality or quantity matters more [2][3][4].
infobox: 27 lb (12 kg) lost in two months

paras: Haub's experiment replaced conventional meals with packaged snacks eaten at intervals, while he restricted total calorie intake. The foods named in coverage include Twinkies, Oreos, Doritos, Little Debbie snack cakes, cereals, cookies and brownies [1]. He stated that he wanted to show that pure calorie counting is what matters most for weight loss [1].

The nickname overstates the junk-food share, since the daily routine also included a protein shake, canned green beans or celery stalks, a multivitamin, whole milk, carrots and vitamin-fortified cereal [1].

On T Nation, the diet appears in passing in several long-running threads. One poster says it 'works' because a food environment full of calorie-dense products makes any intervention that reduces intake lead to fat loss [2]. Another describes it as having worked because the experimenter was controlling portions, adding that the baseline population is not healthy and almost any dietary change would benefit the average person [3].

A different thread participant says he had contacted Haub years earlier to discuss the research [4]. Other mentions use the diet as a joke or contrast to strict plans such as carnivore or ketogenic eating [5][6].
No studies found. The experiment was a self-experiment by one person reported in news coverage rather than a controlled trial [1].

lore.intro: On T Nation the Twinkie diet is a common shorthand in debates about calories versus food quality [2][3].

claims.claim: Fat loss comes down to calories, so the food source does not matter for the scale.
Any dietary intervention helps the average person because baseline diets are poor.

timeline.event: Mark Haub follows his convenience-store diet for about two months and loses 27 lb [1].
